newsitem.title: USA: Anchorage airport sees cargo boom.
newsitem.headline: Anchorage airport sees cargo boom.

text.p: Anchorage International Airport's location has long made it a quick pit stop for aircraft, but with new special status received from the government it is hoping to become a major cargo center.
"It is important for people to realize that Anchorage is ready to capitalize on the globalization of the air cargo market," Morton Plumb, the airport's director, told Reuters Thursday.
"We want to be more than a transit refueling point," Patricia Eckert, the airport's marketing director, said.

Anchorage, which is midway between North America, Asia and Europe on the great circle route, already has more than 30 freighter operators using the aiport. It averages about 420 cargo landings per week, according to the airport's statistics.

Anchorage was the world's 10th largest cargo airport in 1996, handling 1,269,283 tons of cargo, an increase of nearly 30 percent from 1995, according to the statistics compiled by the Airports Council International. Chicago was 11th and Seoul was 9th.

But in November, U.S. Transportation Department quietly issued an order which allows international carriers to expand cargo tranfer activites. Foreign carriers can now take cargo off planes and transfer it to another of their aircraft or to another airline.
This permits the foreign carriers to essentially create sorting and distribution hubs at Alaska airports, according to Eckert.
Carriers from Japan and the United Kingdom are not yet allowed, because of bilateral aviation negotiations.
"DOT is providing us with essentially open skies for cargo," Plumb said. "This doesn't necessarily bring more traffic but it lets the traffic that is already here be more efficient."

Interest has been strong already, Eckert said. Anchorage International has already had "informal discussions" with Japan Airlines, Nippon Cargo Airlines, Korean Air and Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd. to do more than refuel, she said.
Three developers have submitted plans for cargo buildings that could total as much as 850,000 additional square feet of cargo warehouse space.
Current freighter users of the airport, including Federal Express Corp, United Parcel Service, and United Airlines are all expanding facilities.
UPS this month dedicated its newly expanded Anchorage hub, which jumped to 94,800 square feet from 31,200 square feet, Ken Shapero, UPS spokesman said.
"It is a staging point for Asia and North America," he said, "flights from the U.S. hubs, Asia and Europe are converging there," he said.
"It is a transfer hub for us. We are sorting containers, we are not sorting individual packages," Shapero said. "It is also a cargo transfer point," he said.
"Anchorage is becoming more important for us," he said, Asia is beginning to boil."

Federal Express uses Anchorage as its Asian gateway and earlier this month broke ground on a $38 million expansion that will take its facility from 208,000 to 335,000 square feet, according to Jess Bunn, Fed Ex spokesman.
The enlarged facility will be capable of sorting 10,400 packages per hour, more than double the current 4,400 per hour.
"We expect as our Asia business grows we will be doing more business in Anchorage," Bunn said.
United Airlines, which just launched freighter service, will use Anchorage as its hub, according to Eckert and has 105 crew based in Anchorage.
